title: Platform guardrails in Azure OpenAI and Foundry
summary: A Foundry guardrail is a named set of controls. Each control names a risk, the intervention points to scan and an action. Models and agents follow different rules, and streaming mode decides when violating text can appear.
useIf: You deploy models or agents in Microsoft Foundry and want managed filtering configured as policy, not code.
avoidIf: Your agents run outside Foundry Agent Service or your policy needs custom taxonomies: guardrails do not cover other registered agents.

explain.md: A **guardrail** is a named collection of controls. Each control defines a risk, the intervention points to scan (user input, tool call, tool response, output) and the response action: **annotate** or **annotate and block**. Agents support only annotate and block. Tool call and tool response controls are preview and for agents only. The system applies to all Foundry Models sold by Azure except audio transcription models, and to agents built in Foundry Agent Service, not to other agents in the Foundry Control Plane [[r1]]. New models get `Microsoft.DefaultV2` [[r2]]. Creating guardrails needs the Foundry Account Owner role, renamed from Azure AI Account Owner [[r1]].

explain.title: An agent guardrail replaces the model guardrail
explain.md: Risks are detected in an agent using the guardrail assigned to the agent, not the one on its underlying model. With no custom guardrail the agent inherits the model's. Controls for preview risks that agents do not yet support are ignored for the agent but still apply to models that share the guardrail [[r1]].

**Streaming.** The default mode buffers completion text, filters each buffer and returns content chunks, not single tokens. The **asynchronous filter** streams token by token with no added filter latency, sends annotations in separate messages with offsets, and guarantees the stop signal only within about a 1,000 character window, so some violating text can reach the user first. Changing the mode needs permission to modify content filtering policies [[r9]]. The Foundry **PII filter** scans model output only, is preview, and its block action blocks the whole output [[r8]].

whereToUse: Applying one policy consistently across many model deployments and agents

Giving security teams a named policy object to review and audit

use: Use the default guardrail as a baseline and add controls by risk
Use agent guardrails with tool call and tool response controls for agents with tools
Use buffered streaming when showing violating text even briefly is unacceptable
Use annotate mode first to measure flag rates before blocking
avoid: Avoid assuming a model guardrail covers an agent that has its own guardrail
Avoid enabling groundedness or Spotlighting controls and expecting them to run on agents
Avoid the asynchronous filter for audiences where early exposure is unacceptable
flips: Latency matters more than brief exposure and the audience is internal: asynchronous streaming is acceptable
Agents run outside Foundry Agent Service: implement guards in your own pipeline
Policy needs custom categories or languages not tested by the service: add your own classifier

pitfalls.symptom: Tool calls are unscanned after creating an agent guardrail
pitfalls.cause: The agent's guardrail fully overrides the model's and contained no tool controls
pitfalls.fix: Add tool call and tool response controls to the agent guardrail

pitfalls.symptom: A groundedness control seems inactive on an agent
pitfalls.cause: Groundedness and Spotlighting are not applicable to agents, so the control does not take effect
pitfalls.fix: Check the applicability table and add a separate groundedness step for agents

pitfalls.symptom: Users briefly see disallowed text while streaming
pitfalls.cause: Asynchronous filter signals the stop only within about 1,000 characters
pitfalls.fix: Use buffered streaming for sensitive audiences, or hide text client-side until clear

pitfalls.symptom: An agent has no guardrail despite the organisation policy
pitfalls.cause: The agent is registered in the Foundry Control Plane but not built in Foundry Agent Service
pitfalls.fix: Add guards in the agent's own pipeline or rebuild it in the service

scenarios.title: Streaming chat for teenagers
scenarios.situation: A public chat product for teenagers streams responses for a responsive feel. Showing even a few harmful sentences is unacceptable to the business. Latency complaints are secondary.
scenarios.question: Which streaming mode do you choose?

options.name: Default buffered streaming with filtering on each buffer
options.why: Content is filtered before chunks reach the user, so no violating text is shown.

options.name: Asynchronous filter with the client hiding text until annotations arrive
options.tradeoff: You build the hiding logic, and the stop signal is only guaranteed within about 1,000 characters.

options.name: Asynchronous filter with raw rendering
options.why: Violating text can be displayed before the stop signal.
options.tradeoff: Right for an internal tool where brief exposure is tolerable.

flips.if: Audience is internal staff and speed matters
flips.then: Asynchronous streaming with logging is acceptable.
Non-streamed responses avoid the issue entirely.

scenarios.takeaway: Streaming mode is a decision about tolerated exposure.

scenarios.title: Foundry agent with external tools
scenarios.situation: An agent in Foundry Agent Service calls a CRM tool and a web-fetch tool. The team set guardrails on the model deployment months ago and now builds the agent. Preview features are acceptable.
unknowns: Do all controls the team uses apply to agents?
scenarios.question: How do you configure the guardrail?

options.name: A dedicated agent guardrail with user input, tool call, tool response and output controls using annotate and block
options.why: Agents use their own guardrail, and the tool controls are the only managed scan of tool traffic.
options.tradeoff: Preview features and block-only actions for agents.

options.name: Inherit the model's guardrail and enforce tool allow lists in code
options.why: Keeps input and output coverage and limits tool abuse deterministically.
options.tradeoff: No managed scan of tool calls and responses.

options.name: An agent guardrail containing only an output control
options.why: It replaces the model's controls and leaves input, tool calls and tool responses unscanned.
options.tradeoff: Right only for an agent with no tools and trusted input.

flips.if: Preview is not allowed for tool controls
flips.then: Use deterministic allow lists and the standalone APIs inside your tool wrapper.

scenarios.takeaway: Review the agent's effective guardrail, not the model's.

quiz.q: A model deployment has a strict violence control. An agent on that model has its own guardrail without a violence control. What applies to the agent?
options: Only the agent's guardrail, so no violence control
quiz.explain: The agent's guardrail fully overrides the model's, so the model's violence control does not apply. Guardrails are not combined, and the default applies only when no custom guardrail is assigned.

quiz.q: How long is the stop signal guaranteed to arrive in the asynchronous filter?
quiz.explain: The docs guarantee the stop signal only within about a 1,000 character window, so some violating text can be shown first. It is not before tokens, not time-based and not only at the end.

quiz.q: Which controls are listed as not applicable to agents?
quiz.explain: Spotlighting and groundedness apply to models only. Task adherence and the harm categories apply to both models and agents.

flashcards.back: A named collection of controls. Each defines a risk, intervention points to scan and an action (annotate, or annotate and block).
An agent's guardrail fully overrides its model's. With none assigned, the agent inherits the model's. Applies only to agents built in Foundry Agent Service.
Default buffers and filters each chunk. Asynchronous sends tokens immediately and signals stop only within about 1,000 characters.
